parts.note: a two-word call to look, read as an old-fashioned command to observe something remarkable

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be shown what they are supposed to be looking at.
explanation.walkthrough: A visual trick: in print 'what?' appears in bold type, so EH (what?) sits in BOLD, giving B-EH-OLD, and 'See' defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an archaic imperative meaning look or observe, often used to draw attention.

parts.note: in Scotland 'heavy' is a dark ale, so a container of heavy is a cask for ale, not just a weighty box

explanation.surface: A large weighty box or crate.
explanation.walkthrough: HEAVY is a Scottish name for a kind of bitter beer, so the 'heavy container' is a cask holding beer, though the surface suggests merely something weighty.
explanation.definitionFit: A cask for ale holds 'heavy', the Scottish term for a strong dark ale, and is itself famously weighty.

indicators.note: in says the letters for one and leaves sit inside the short form for house

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
pp is the abbreviation for pages, and pages are leaves of a book

explanation.surface: A creature that someone moves into a home, or that departs from one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' looks like a verb but is a noun: book leaves are pages, abbreviated pp.
explanation.definitionFit: A large African river mammal is an animal.

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters for the score are read from bottom to top

parts.note: a ten-nil scoreline is said as TEN NIL

indicators.note: start to means just the opening letter of the word substitute is taken

explanation.surface: A football team leading ten-nil brings on substitutes on the wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses TENNIL to LINNET; the first letter of 'substitute' adds S. 'wingers' looks like footballers but means birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Small finches are birds, creatures with wings, hence wingers.

clue.text: How stupid soccer bosses relax, hiding Euro pressure

parts.note: the FA, the Football Association, runs English soccer

indicators.note: hiding means the letters for Euro and pressure are concealed inside the word for relax

parts.note: to relax is to calm down, so calm
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Football's governing body takes it easy and dodges a European pressure campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How stupid' is a definition by example: the gesture expresses those words. The FA (Football Association) is English football's governing body.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting a palm to the forehead is the gesture that signals someone thinks something is foolish.

clue.text: A prison full of charming and extremely close contact

indicators.note: full of means the word for prison is stuffed with the word for charming

parts.note: can is slang for a prison
quaint means charming in an old-fashioned way

indicators.note: extremely means the outer letters of close are used, first and last

explanation.surface: A jail full of charm and very near connections.
explanation.walkthrough: CAN is US slang for prison; 'full of' puts QUAINT inside it, and 'extremely' takes the first and last letters of 'close'.
explanation.definitionFit: A contact is someone you know, a person you have met socially or through work.

clue.text: Fluid most unlikely to be found in cracked ice

indicators.note: found in says the word for most unlikely sits inside the scrambled letters of ice
cracked suggests ice broken up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the last person to do something is the most unlikely to

explanation.surface: A liquid that would hardly ever turn up in broken ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracked' rearranges ICE to E and IC, and 'found in' sets LAST between them. 'most unlikely' is read as the last person to do something.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something flexible and adaptable, not rigid.

indicators.note: into says the rearranged letters go inside the word for rear

parts.note: ass is slang for the backside or rear

indicators.note: garbage describes something mangled, so the letters of loaded are scrambled

explanation.surface: Rubbish piled into the back of a truck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'garbage' looks like a noun but rearranges LOADED to ADEADLO; 'into' places it inside ASS, slang for the rear.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete write-off is something with no worth or purpose at all.

parts.note: May is one of the months of the year

explanation.surface: A broadcaster who is only a month old.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Mayo is a long-serving BBC radio presenter.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Mayo is a well-known British radio broadcaster, so the surname names a presenter.

parts.note: ex means former or old
and means with, joining things together

explanation.surface: A retired cleric carrying a balloon.
explanation.definitionFit: To balloon is to swell or grow larger, as a verb.

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the word for crouch is dropped

parts.note: to squat is to crouch down
to count on someone is to rely on them

explanation.surface: Crouching to count the dead.
explanation.walkthrough: As in 'dead centre': dead means exactly or directly. 'mostly' cuts SQUAT to SQUA.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead can mean exactly or directly, as in hitting something dead in the middle.

clue.text: You all clear about business magazine?

indicators.note: about means the letters for you and all clear go around the short form for business

parts.note: thee is the old form of you
no mist means the air is all clear
Co is the abbreviation for company, a business

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether everyone understands a business publication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all clear' is read literally as NO MIST; THEE and NOMIST together wrap CO. The question mark admits the answer is one title among business magazines.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running London weekly on finance and world affairs is a periodical; the question mark marks it as one example.

clue.text: How Dambusters may be seen — very low

definitions.meaning: the word Dambusters has BUST, meaning broken, at its centre

explanation.walkthrough: The Dambusters were the RAF squadron that breached German dams in 1943; read the word itself and its middle letters spell BUST, i.e. it is broken in the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone grief-stricken is utterly miserable, deep in sorrow; the first reading is a word whose middle is bust.

clue.text: 1A fund keeps up site of naval base

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the whole string of letters is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the answer to 1 across means see, which is also lo
a pot is a fund of money, as in a jackpot
saves means keeps

explanation.surface: A fund holding money in reserve for a naval site.
explanation.walkthrough: '1A' refers to 1 across, whose sense 'see!' is also LO. 'up' reverses LO + POT + SAVES to give the Crimean port.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crimean port city has long been the base of Russia's Black Sea Fleet.

indicators.note: opening means the word for ceremony is split open to take the other letters

parts.note: a rite is a ceremony

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the word for swanky is dropped

parts.note: posh means swanky or smart

explanation.surface: A smart, grand opening event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejoin' is not join again but reply. 'mostly' cuts POSH to POS, and 'opening' splits RITE to take it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rejoinder is a quick retort, a sharp reply.

clue.text: Head of state fixes up accommodation for reporters

parts.note: pres is short for president, a head of state

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word for fixes is read from bottom to top

parts.note: moors means fixes, as a boat is moored

explanation.surface: A president arranges lodging for journalists.
explanation.definitionFit: The room set aside for journalists at a venue or event.

indicators.note: short means the last letter of the word for kiss is dropped

parts.note: to neck is to kiss
Rose is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Kissing a girl briefly, then death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts NECK to NEC.
explanation.definitionFit: Tissue that undergoes necrosis dies, decaying in the body.

clue.text: Dance music chosen — that's right, love

parts.note: elect means chosen
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Someone picks dance music and declares it correct, with affection.
explanation.definitionFit: A style of electronic dance music with a heavy synth beat.

clue.text: Shadow boxing a very painful exercise

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing, so the word for shadow holds the other letters

parts.note: to shadow someone is to trail them

explanation.surface: Shadow boxing is a punishing workout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxing' puts A + V inside TRAIL, giving TR-AV-AIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Toil or hard labour is gruelling, painful effort.

clue.text: Gold rush area in US city

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a gust is a sudden rush of wind

explanation.surface: A gold rush region in an American town.
explanation.walkthrough: A city in Georgia, home of the Masters golf, and also the capital of Maine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Georgia golfing town and the capital of Maine are American cities.

indicators.note: rock means shake, so the letters of real and big are rearranged

explanation.surface: A real big name in rock music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' is the anagram signal on REAL BIG; Peter Gabriel was Genesis's singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Gabriel is a famous English singer and songwriter.

clue.text: MPs who can't be said to be corrupt?

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or altered, so the letters of who can't be said are rearranged

parts.note: opposition frontbenchers hold no office, so they have no power to abuse

explanation.surface: Members of Parliament whose honesty is beyond question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrupt' looks like the point of the sentence but is the anagram signal on WHO CANT BE SAID; 'to be' only links. The apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: The opposition's team of spokespeople are all members of Parliament.

indicators.note: Partially says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Giving a grubby backside a partial wipe.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest point of anything is its bottom.

indicators.note: in a down clue thrown up means the word for stuff is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to cram is to stuff

explanation.surface: Something vomited turns out to be brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit distilled from grape pulp left after winemaking.

indicators.note: comic means funny or absurd, signalling a jumbled version of the letters

explanation.surface: A comedian boasting of a racy, spicy act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comic' looks like a noun for the actor but rearranges ACTOR + IM to ROMATIC, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: Spices give off a strong pleasant scent.

definitions.meaning: to bring to a conclusion, close
a tease or a prank played on someone

explanation.definitionFit: As a phrasal verb it means conclude; as a noun it means a joke or deception.

indicators.note: in says the Roman fifty sits inside the word for battle

parts.note: to battle is to compete
L is fifty in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Fifty people put to death in a war.
explanation.definitionFit: To execute a task is to carry it out fully.

clue.text: Extremely peaceful river or rivers, for example

indicators.note: extremely means the first and last letters of peaceful are taken

parts.note: the Ural is a river flowing from Russia into the Caspian

explanation.surface: A very calm river, or several of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' gives PL, the outer letters of peaceful. 'rivers' is an example of a word in its many-of-a-kind form.
explanation.definitionFit: The word rivers is an instance of a noun in its more-than-one grammatical number.
